title: Shamita Shetty Opens Up About Endometriosis, Surgery, and the Two Years It Took to Lose 5 Kg
excerpt: On Soha Ali Khan's podcast, the actor described sudden weight gain, pain that woke her from sleep, and a diagnosis that came only after years of dismissed symptoms.
body:
• Shamita Shetty gained 4-5 kg — the heaviest she had ever been — before being diagnosed with endometriosis, a condition that had caused her ovary to adhere to her rectum.
  • Multiple doctors missed the diagnosis; only specialist Dr. Neeta Warty identified the condition through the correct imaging protocol.
  • Recovery from laparoscopic surgery took months, and Shetty says it took her two years to lose the weight she gained during the illness.
  • Endometriosis affects approximately 190 million women worldwide, with an average diagnostic delay of 7-10 years.

Shamita Shetty, the Bollywood actor and Bigg Boss finalist, has given one of the most candid celebrity accounts of living with endometriosis in a new episode of Soha Ali Khan's podcast All About Her.

In the conversation, Shetty described a years-long journey of dismissed symptoms, overlapping conditions, and a diagnosis that came only after the disease had progressed significantly — a pattern medical experts say is devastatingly common for the estimated 190 million women worldwide who live with the condition.

"My Body Was Telling Me Something Was Wrong"

Shetty told Khan that she first noticed symptoms she could not explain — pain during intercourse, abnormal bleeding, and a persistent sense that something was off. But initial tests came back normal.

"When those symptoms came back, I thought maybe it was normal. It's part and parcel of being a woman," she said. "Certain things are normalised with us, whether it's period pain, anything related to our hormones. We are just expected to go through that."

She also experienced rapid weight gain — 4-5 kilograms — the heaviest she had ever been, along with significant water retention. Complicating matters, she was simultaneously going through perimenopause, making it impossible to distinguish which symptoms belonged to which condition.

"I kept telling my trainer over and over again, 'There's something wrong.' Sometimes I'd burst into tears because I just knew something wasn't right, even though I couldn't explain it," Shetty recalled.

The Diagnosis That Changed Everything

It was only when she consulted Dr. Neeta Warty, a specialist actively involved in endometriosis detection research with India's National Institute for Research in Reproductive Health, that the condition was identified.

Dr. Warty ordered the correct imaging protocol — not a routine MRI, but specialized scans that revealed the full extent of the disease. The endometriosis had grown to the point where Shetty's ovary had become stuck to her rectum, a complication that develops over time when the condition goes undiagnosed.

"That doesn't happen overnight," Shetty said. "It takes time."

Surgery and a Long Recovery

Shetty underwent laparoscopic surgery, but the recovery was far more grueling than she anticipated.

"I was like an old woman for a while. I was walking, stopping, panting. Even after 6-8 weeks, it took me a while to get my strength back and have the guts to go and do a leg workout."

— Shamita Shetty

While her surgeon had estimated a 4-6 week recovery window, Shetty says it took months to regain her stamina, and a full two years to lose the 5 kilograms she had gained during the illness.

Why This Conversation Matters

Endometriosis has an average diagnostic delay of 7-10 years globally. In India and across South Asian communities abroad, discussions around menstrual and reproductive health remain heavily stigmatized, often delaying diagnosis even further.

Dr. Warty, who joined Shetty on the podcast, emphasized that persistent pelvic pain, painful periods, and pain during intercourse are not conditions women should simply endure. Early diagnosis through proper imaging can prevent the kind of organ damage Shetty experienced.

For Indian women in the diaspora — many of whom navigate cultural expectations around silence on reproductive health — hearing a public figure describe these symptoms openly can be the difference between seeking medical attention and suffering quietly for years longer.
